blocks.cap: Every value between \(4{,}700\) and \(4{,}800\) leans toward whichever landmark it is closer to, and the dashed midpoint at \(4{,}750\) is the referee that calls it. Because \(4{,}732\) lands in the bottom half it stays at \(4{,}700\), while \(4{,}768\) lands in the top half and ticks up to \(4{,}800\). The shortcut is the boxed tens digit. A \(3\) means you are under \(50\) and still in the bottom half, a \(6\) means you have reached \(50\) and crossed into the top half, so reading that one digit tells you which side of the referee you are on without walking the whole line.

blocks.x: A 3D printer reads \(7.83\) m of filament remaining. Round to the nearest tenth. The hundredths digit \(3\) decides. What is \(7.83\) rounded to the nearest tenth?
hints: Your two neighbors are \(7.8\) and \(7.9\), and the line between them is at \(7.85\). The only digit that decides which neighbor you get is the hundredths digit, the one right after the tenths place.
The hundredths digit of \(7.83\) is \(3\). Since \(7.83\) is below the midpoint \(7.85\), it stays with the lower neighbor. Keep the tenths digit as it is and drop the rest.
blocks.sol: The tenths on either side of \(7.83\) are \(7.8\) and \(7.9\), and the midpoint is \(7.85\). The hundredths digit is \(3\), so the reading sits below the midpoint and stays with the lower neighbor. Keep the tenths digit and drop the rest, giving \(\boxed{7.8}\).

blocks.x: A tide gauge reads \(3.617\) m. The harbor chart records to the nearest hundredth. The thousandths digit \(7\) decides. Round \(3.617\) to the nearest hundredth.
hints: You only care about which side of the midpoint \(3.615\) the reading falls on. Compare \(3.617\) to \(3.615\). Is it below the midpoint, at the midpoint, or above it?

The digit that decides everything is the one just past the hundredths place, the thousandths digit. Here that digit is \(7\). Anything \(5\) or higher tips you up to the larger neighbor, so keep two digits after the point and bump the hundredths up.
blocks.sol: The hundredths on either side of \(3.617\) are \(3.61\) and \(3.62\), and the midpoint is \(3.615\). The thousandths digit is \(7\), which is \(5\) or more, so round up. The harbor chart records \(\boxed{3.62}\). The distances agree, since \(3.617\) is \(0.007\) above \(3.61\) but only \(0.003\) below \(3.62\).

blocks.x: A lab scale reads \(1.995\) grams. Round to the nearest hundredth. The thousandths digit \(5\) is a tie, so round up. The hundredths digit is \(9\), triggering a carry. What is the result?
hints: The deciding digit is the thousandths digit, the \(5\) in \(1.99\underline{5}\). A \(5\) is the exact halfway case, so round the hundredths place up to the larger value. The only catch is that the digit you are bumping is a \(9\), so think about where it goes when it cannot just become a \(10\).

Bumping the hundredths \(9\) up writes a \(0\) there and carries \(1\) into the tenths place. But the tenths digit is also \(9\), so it becomes \(0\) and carries \(1\) into the ones place, turning \(1\) into \(2\). So \(1.99\) climbs to \(2.00\). Keep both decimal places.
blocks.sol: Keeping two decimal places makes the thousandths digit the decider, and here it is \(5\) with nothing behind it, an exact tie. So the hundredths place rounds up. That digit is a \(9\), so it becomes \(0\) and carries \(1\) into the tenths, which is also \(9\), so that becomes \(0\) and carries into the ones, lifting the \(1\) to a \(2\). $$1.995 \approx \boxed{2.00}$$ Keep both zeros, since the notebook still records two decimal places.

blocks.x: The rounding rule. To round to a place, look at the single digit just after it, the deciding digit. If it is $5$ or more the place ticks up. If $4$ or less it stays. Either way, every digit after the rounding place drops to zero. You never have to measure the gap to the midpoint, because that one digit already tells you which half you are in. When the deciding digit is exactly $5$ with nothing but zeros behind it, the value sits dead on the midpoint, a tie, and this course sends every tie to the larger value. One wrinkle. If the place you are bumping is a $9$, it cannot climb, so it rolls over to $0$ and carries $1$ into the next place left, exactly like carrying in addition, and if that carry runs off the front the number gains a whole digit, the way $9.96$ rounds to $10.0$.
A freezer reads \(-83\) degrees. Round to the nearest ten. The neighbors are \(-90\) and \(-80\). Measure each gap and pick the closer one. What is the result?
hints: Find the gap from \(-83\) to each neighbor. How far is it left to \(-90\), and how far right to \(-80\)? The shorter trip wins.
From \(-83\) it is \(7\) steps left to reach \(-90\), but only \(3\) steps right to reach \(-80\). The nearer multiple of ten is \(-80\).
blocks.sol: The multiples of ten around \(-83\) are \(-90\) and \(-80\). The gap down to \(-90\) is \(7\), and the gap up to \(-80\) is only \(3\), so the technician records \(\boxed{-80}\) degrees. Negatives use the same midpoint test as positives. The midpoint here is \(-85\), and \(-83\) sits to the right of it.

blocks.x: A thermostat reads \(-2.35\) degrees. Round to the nearest tenth. \(-2.35\) is the exact midpoint between \(-2.4\) and \(-2.3\). The tie rule rounds to the larger value. What does the display show?
hints: Forget the minus sign for a second and just picture the number line. Mark \(-2.4\) on the left and \(-2.3\) on the right, then drop \(-2.35\) in between. Is it closer to one of them, or stuck dead in the middle?

It is a perfect tie, so use the rule, round to the larger value. "Larger" means farther to the right on the number line. Between \(-2.4\) and \(-2.3\), the one on the right is \(-2.3\), so that is your answer.
blocks.sol: The tenths around \(-2.35\) are \(-2.4\) and \(-2.3\), and \(-2.35\) is \(0.05\) from each, so it is an exact tie. A tie rounds to the larger value, and the larger of two negatives is the one farther right. The display shows \(\boxed{-2.3}\). It feels backwards because \(2.3\) is less than \(2.4\), but with the minus signs attached, \(-2.3\) is the bigger number.

blocks.x: Rounding negatives. A negative number is not a special case with its own rulebook. It rounds to the nearer multiple exactly like a positive one, and the only thing to watch is what larger means for negatives. Larger always means farther to the right on the number line, so between two negatives the larger one is the one closer to zero. When a negative value lands exactly on a midpoint, the same round-to-the-larger tie rule sends you toward zero, which is why $-2.35$ rounds to $-2.3$ and not $-2.4$.
Three crates weigh \(487\), \(213\), and \(356\) kg. Round each to the nearest hundred, then add the rounded values. What is your estimated total?
hints: Handle one crate at a time. Look at the part of each weight after the hundreds and decide whether it pushes the number up to the next hundred or leaves it at the hundred below.
Round each one. \(487\) is past the halfway mark so it becomes \(500\), \(213\) is below halfway so it becomes \(200\), and \(356\) is past halfway so it becomes \(400\). Now add \(500 + 200 + 400\).
blocks.sol: For \(487\), the leftover past the hundred is \(87\), above \(50\), so it rounds up to \(500\). For \(213\) the leftover is \(13\), so it stays at \(200\). For \(356\) the leftover is \(56\), so it rounds up to \(400\). Adding gives \(500 + 200 + 400 = \boxed{1100}\). The exact total is \(1{,}056\), so the estimate tells you instantly whether the van is near its limit.

blocks.x: A field-trip invoice lists \(29\) students at \(6.10\) dollars each, printing \(1{,}769\) dollars. Round each to a friendly value and multiply. What is your quick estimate of \(29 \times 6.10\)?
hints: You are not finding the exact total here, you are building a quick comparison number. Replace each part with a friendly nearby value first. What is \(29\) rounded to the nearest ten, and what is \(6.10\) rounded to the nearest whole dollar?

Rounding \(29\) to the nearest ten gives \(30\), since \(29\) is much closer to \(30\) than to \(20\). Rounding \(6.10\) to the nearest whole dollar gives \(6\), since \(6.10\) is just past \(6\). Now multiply \(30 \times 6\).
blocks.sol: \(29\) rounds to \(30\) at the nearest ten, and \(6.10\) rounds to \(6\) at the nearest dollar, since \(10\) cents is nowhere near the \(6.50\) midpoint. Multiplying the friendly numbers gives \(30 \times 6 = \boxed{180}\). The printed \(1{,}769\) is about ten times that, the signature of a decimal point that slipped one spot. The exact total is \(176.90\).

blocks.x: Estimation as an error-check. Round each piece to a friendly value before you combine them, and you get a quick ballpark close enough to catch a real mistake. Because it is only a ballpark, write it with $\approx$, like $29 \times 6.10 \approx 180$, never an equals sign. The payoff is speed with a safety net. When a printed total like $1{,}769$ lands ten times away from your estimate of about $180$, you know something is wrong before doing any careful work. Rounding trades a little accuracy for a lot of speed, which is exactly what makes it good for checking answers and for mental math.
In 1856 surveyors measured Everest and got exactly \(29{,}000\) feet. Worried a round number would look like a guess, they published \(29{,}002\) feet, inventing two feet to appear more precise.
A gauge is rounded to the nearest tenth and reports \(4.3\) mm. The original reading was stored to two decimal places. What is the largest two-decimal value that still rounds to \(4.3\)?
hints: The reported \(4.3\) covers everything from \(4.25\) up to but not including \(4.35\). You only need the values in that stretch that have exactly two decimal places, so start at the top end and step downward.

Check \(4.35\) first. It sits exactly halfway between \(4.3\) and \(4.4\), so by the larger-value rule it rounds up to \(4.4\), not \(4.3\). That means \(4.35\) is out. Step down one hundredth to \(4.34\) and round it to the nearest tenth to see where it lands.
blocks.sol: A reported \(4.3\) covers everything from \(4.25\) up to just under \(4.35\), because \(4.35\) is a tie that rounds up to \(4.4\) instead. The largest two-decimal value in that stretch is \(\boxed{4.34}\), whose hundredths digit \(4\) sends it down to \(4.3\). The band is half-open, so the lower end is included and the upper end is not.

blocks.x: Rounding is one-way. The moment you round, you trade one exact number for a tidier one and the original is gone for good. A rounded $4.3$ no longer stands for a single value. It stands for a whole stretch, everything from the lower midpoint $4.25$ up to just under the upper midpoint $4.35$, since every original in that band rounds back to $4.3$. That is why rounding is a one-way street. Many different originals funnel down to the same rounded value, so you can never run it backward. The most you can ever say in reverse is name the two boundaries the original had to live between.
A price rounds to \(7\) at the nearest dollar, to \(6.8\) at the nearest tenth, and its hundredths digit is \(0\). Exactly one price to the cent satisfies all three. What is it?
hints: Turn each clue into an interval. Rounding to the nearest whole dollar gives \(7\), so the price runs from \(6.5\) up to just under \(7.5\). Rounding to the nearest tenth gives \(6.8\), so the price runs from \(6.75\) up to just under \(6.85\). The price must sit inside both ranges at once, which means inside the tighter one.

The overlap of the two ranges is \(6.75\) up to just under \(6.85\). Now list the prices in that band whose hundredths digit is \(0\). The candidates ending in zero cents are \(6.80\). Check the only one that lands in the band.
blocks.sol: Rounding to \(7\) at the nearest dollar means \(6.5 \le p < 7.5\). Rounding to \(6.8\) at the nearest tenth means \(6.75 \le p < 6.85\), which sits entirely inside the first range. The prices to the cent in that band run \(6.75\) through \(6.84\), and the only one with a hundredths digit of \(0\) is \(\boxed{6.80}\). Turning each rounding clue into a range and overlapping them is the standard way to pin a value down.

review.x: A scoreboard reads \(7{,}284\) fans. The press box reports to the nearest hundred. What is \(7{,}284\) rounded to the nearest hundred?
hints: Find the two multiples of one hundred that hug \(7{,}284\). One is below it and one is above it. What are they?
The midpoint sits halfway between those two multiples. Compare \(7{,}284\) to that midpoint. Is the count below the line or above it?
review.sol: The hundreds around \(7{,}284\) are \(7{,}200\) and \(7{,}300\), and the midpoint is \(7{,}250\). Since \(7{,}284\) is above the midpoint, it climbs, and the press box reports \(\boxed{7300}\) fans.

review.x: A fundraiser total of \(3{,}500\) dollars is to be printed rounded to the nearest thousand. \(3{,}500\) is the exact midpoint. Using the half-way-up rule, what goes on the banner?
hints: The two nearest thousands are \(3{,}000\) and \(4{,}000\). Where does \(3{,}500\) sit relative to those two markers?
It sits exactly halfway, so neither one is closer. When that happens, our rule says to pick the larger of the two thousands.
review.sol: \(3{,}500\) is \(500\) from \(3{,}000\) and \(500\) from \(4{,}000\), so neither thousand is closer. That is an exact tie, and our rule sends a tie to the larger value, so the banner reads \(\boxed{4000}\).

review.x: A scale reads \(6.47\) kg. A recipe records to the nearest tenth. Round \(6.47\) to the nearest tenth.
hints: You are rounding to the tenths place, so look at the next digit to its right, the hundredths digit, to decide what happens.
The hundredths digit is 7. Since 7 is 5 or more, the tenths digit goes up by one.
review.sol: The tenths around \(6.47\) are \(6.4\) and \(6.5\), and the midpoint is \(6.45\). The hundredths digit is \(7\), which is \(5\) or more, so the tenths digit goes up by one and \(6.47\) rounds to \(\boxed{6.5}\).

review.x: A lap is timed at \(0.382\) seconds. The results sheet keeps two decimal places. Round \(0.382\) to the nearest hundredth.
hints: Rounding to the nearest hundredth means keeping two decimal places, so look at the next digit to the right, the thousandths digit.
The thousandths digit in \(0.382\) is \(2\). Since \(2\) is less than \(5\), the hundredths digit stays the same and you drop everything after it.
review.sol: The hundredths around \(0.382\) are \(0.38\) and \(0.39\), and the midpoint is \(0.385\). The thousandths digit is \(2\), below \(5\), so the hundredths digit stays and everything after it is dropped, giving \(\boxed{0.38}\). The gaps confirm it, \(0.002\) down versus \(0.008\) up.

review.x: A bus ride takes exactly \(9.5\) minutes. The schedule lists whole minutes only. \(9.5\) is exactly halfway between \(9\) and \(10\). What whole number does the schedule show?
hints: Find the two whole numbers \(9.5\) sits between. How far is it from each one?
It is exactly the same distance from \(9\) and from \(10\), so it is a tie. The half-way rule sends a tie to the larger value.
review.sol: \(9.5\) is \(0.5\) from \(9\) and \(0.5\) from \(10\), so it is an exact tie. A tie rounds to the larger value, so the schedule lists the trip as \(\boxed{10}\) minutes.

review.x: A fitness band reads \(0.65\) battery and rounds to one decimal place. \(0.65\) is exactly halfway between \(0.6\) and \(0.7\). What does the band display?
hints: The two tenths on either side of \(0.65\) are \(0.6\) and \(0.7\). Which one is \(0.65\) closer to?
It is not closer to either one, it sits exactly in the middle. The halfway rule says to round to the larger value.
review.sol: \(0.65\) is \(0.05\) from \(0.6\) and \(0.05\) from \(0.7\), so it is a perfect tie. A tie rounds to the larger value, so the fitness band shows \(\boxed{0.7}\).

review.x: A caliper reads \(0.396\) cm and the spec sheet keeps two decimal places. The thousandths digit \(6\) rounds the hundredths \(9\) up, triggering a carry. Round \(0.396\) to the nearest hundredth.
hints: The hundredths place is the second digit after the decimal point. In \(0.396\) that digit is the \(9\). To decide whether it stays or climbs, look at the next digit to its right, the one in the thousandths place.

The thousandths digit is \(6\), which is \(5\) or more, so the hundredths place rounds up. But a \(9\) cannot become a \(10\) on its own. When the \(9\) rounds up it carries, just like \(9 + 1\) in regular addition.
review.sol: The hundredths digit of \(0.396\) is the \(9\), and the thousandths digit \(6\) is at least \(5\), so that \(9\) rounds up. A \(9\) cannot become a single-digit \(10\), so it turns into \(0\) and carries \(1\) into the tenths, taking \(3\) to \(4\). That gives \(\boxed{0.40}\). Keep the trailing zero so the answer still shows the hundredths place the spec sheet asked for.

review.x: A fuel gauge reads \(8.97\) liters and the trip computer shows one decimal place. The tenths digit is \(9\), so rounding it up triggers a carry into the ones. Round \(8.97\) to the nearest tenth.
hints: The hundredths digit is the deciding digit. It is 7, and 7 is at least 5, so the tenths place rounds up.

Rounding up a tenths digit of 9 turns it into 10 tenths. That is a full one, so carry it into the ones place. The 8 becomes 9 and the tenths digit becomes 0. Keep one decimal place to show you rounded to the nearest tenth.
review.sol: The hundredths digit of \(8.97\) is \(7\), which is at least \(5\), so the tenths place rounds up. The tenths digit is already \(9\), so it rolls over to \(0\) and carries \(1\) into the ones, taking the \(8\) to \(9\). The trip computer shows \(\boxed{9.0}\). Write the trailing zero to show the value was rounded to the nearest tenth.

review.x: A wind-chill of \(-46\) degrees is reported to the nearest ten. The two neighboring tens are \(-50\) and \(-40\), with midpoint \(-45\). Which side is \(-46\) on? Round \(-46\) to the nearest ten.
hints: Place \(-46\) between its neighbors \(-50\) and \(-40\). The halfway mark is \(-45\). Is \(-46\) on the side closer to \(-50\) or closer to \(-40\)?
Count the gaps. From \(-46\) to \(-50\) is \(4\) steps, and from \(-46\) to \(-40\) is \(6\) steps. Pick the multiple of ten with the smaller gap.
review.sol: The multiples of ten around \(-46\) are \(-50\) and \(-40\). The gap to \(-50\) is \(4\) and the gap to \(-40\) is \(6\), so \(-46\) rounds to \(\boxed{-50}\). The midpoint is \(-45\), and \(-46\) sits to the left of it, so there is no tie to break.

review.x: An elevation app shows \(-3.5\) m. The value is exactly halfway between \(-4\) and \(-3\). The larger of those two is closer to zero. Round \(-3.5\) to the nearest whole number.
hints: The two whole-meter choices around \(-3.5\) are \(-4\) and \(-3\). On the number line, which one sits farther to the right?
Half-way values round to the larger number. Between \(-4\) and \(-3\), the larger value is \(-3\), since it is closer to zero.
review.sol: \(-3.5\) is exactly halfway between \(-4\) and \(-3\), so closeness cannot decide and the half-way rule takes over. Larger means farther right on the number line, and \(-3\) is right of \(-4\), so the elevation rounds to \(\boxed{-3}\) meters. Between two negatives, the larger one is always the one closer to zero.

review.x: A freezer probe reads \(-1.25\) degrees. The app rounds to the nearest tenth. \(-1.25\) is an exact tie between \(-1.3\) and \(-1.2\). Round to the larger value. What does the app display?
hints: The tenths place is the first digit after the decimal point. The two nearest tenths around \(-1.25\) are \(-1.3\) and \(-1.2\). Which one is more positive, meaning farther to the right on the number line?

The reading is an exact tie, equally far from both choices. The rule here says a tie rounds to the larger value, and on a number line \(-1.2\) sits to the right of \(-1.3\), so \(-1.2\) is the larger one.
review.sol: \(-1.25\) is \(0.05\) from \(-1.3\) and \(0.05\) from \(-1.2\), so it is an exact tie. A tie goes to the larger value, and \(-1.2\) lies to the right of \(-1.3\) on the number line, so the app displays \(\boxed{-1.2}\).

review.x: A concert order lists \(41\) tickets at \(19.80\) dollars each, printing a total of \(81.18\) dollars. Round each to the nearest friendly value and multiply. What is your quick estimate?
hints: Handle each part on its own. For 41, look at the ones digit to decide which ten it sits closest to. For \(19.80\), the cents tell you whether it stays at 19 dollars or climbs to the next whole dollar.
The ones digit of 41 is 1, so 41 rounds down to 40. The cents in \(19.80\) are 80, which is past the halfway mark of 50, so \(19.80\) rounds up to 20. Now multiply \(40 \times 20\).
review.sol: \(41\) has a ones digit of \(1\), so it rounds down to \(40\). \(19.80\) has \(80\) cents, past the \(50\) mark, so it rounds up to \(20\) dollars. Multiplying gives \(40 \times 20 = \boxed{800}\). The printed \(81.18\) is nowhere near that ballpark, so the receipt is almost certainly missing a digit.

review.x: Three boxes weigh \(596\), \(207\), and \(398\) grams. Round each to the nearest hundred, then add. What is the estimated total?
hints: Look at each weight on its own and find the nearest hundred. The tens digit tells you which way to go, and a tens digit of 5 or more rounds up to the larger hundred.
Round all three first, then add. You should be working with 600, 200, and 400.
review.sol: Round each weight to the nearest hundred one at a time. For \(596\), the tens digit is \(9\), which is well past halfway, so it rounds up to \(600\). For \(207\), the tens digit is \(0\), so it rounds down to \(200\). For \(398\), the tens digit is \(9\), so it rounds up to \(400\). Now add the friendly numbers, \(600 + 200 + 400 = 1200\). The estimate clears the \(1000\) gram mark with room to spare. \(\boxed{1200}\)

review.x: A rain gauge stores readings to the nearest hundredth but its display shows the nearest tenth, reading \(5.3\) mm. What is the smallest two-decimal stored value that rounds to \(5.3\)?
hints: The display rounds to the nearest tenth. The tenths on either side of the shown value are \(5.2\) and \(5.3\). Where does the boundary between rounding down to \(5.2\) and up to \(5.3\) sit?
The midpoint between \(5.2\) and \(5.3\) is \(5.25\). By the halfway rule, that exact midpoint rounds up to \(5.3\). Anything even a hundredth smaller, like \(5.24\), would round down to \(5.2\).
review.sol: The tenths around the stored reading are \(5.2\) and \(5.3\), and the midpoint is \(5.25\). By the half-way rule that midpoint rounds up to \(5.3\), while \(5.24\) would drop to \(5.2\). The smallest qualifying value is \(\boxed{5.25}\).

blocks.x: \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) can never stop, because \(3\) is neither \(2\) nor \(5\). Its digits run forever, but they are not random. They fall into a loop, and the remainders in long division are what force that loop.
Long-divide \(1 \div 3\). At each step the remainder decides the next digit. What number is the remainder at the end of every step?
hints: Don't watch the quotient digit, watch what is left over after you subtract. Each step you have some number, you take away the biggest multiple of \(3\) you can, and a small leftover stays behind. Write down that leftover for the first two or three steps and see if it changes.

On step one you compute \(10 - 9 = 1\). On step two you pull down a zero to make \(10\) again, and \(10 - 9 = 1\). The leftover after subtracting is the same single digit every single time. Type that digit.
blocks.sol: Bring down a zero and divide. \(10 \div 3\) gives digit \(3\) with \(10 - 9 = 1\) left over. Bring down another zero and \(10 \div 3\) gives \(3\) again with \(1\) left over. The remainder at the end of every step is \(\boxed{1}\). Since that leftover is the number we started with, the step copies itself forever, which is why \(\tfrac{1}{3} = 0.\overline{3}\).

blocks.x: Long-dividing \(1 \div 7\) cycles through remainders \(1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5\) before \(1\) returns, giving \(\tfrac{1}{7} = 0.\overline{142857}\). How many digits are in the repeating block?
hints: Only \(0\) through \(6\) can ever be a remainder, and \(0\) would stop the decimal. So while it keeps going, every remainder is one of \(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\). The block repeats once a remainder returns, so the longest a block can run before looping is exactly the number of different remainders that show up.

List the remainders in order until one comes back. They are \(1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5\), and then \(1\) appears again. Count how many remainders you went through before that first repeat. That count is the length of the repeating block.
blocks.sol: Follow the remainders. \(10 \div 7\) gives \(1\) remainder \(3\), then \(30 \div 7\) gives \(4\) remainder \(2\), then \(20 \div 7\) gives \(2\) remainder \(6\), then \(60 \div 7\) gives \(8\) remainder \(4\), then \(40 \div 7\) gives \(5\) remainder \(5\), then \(50 \div 7\) gives \(7\) remainder \(1\). The starting remainder is back after six steps, so the block is \(\boxed{6}\) digits long, namely \(142857\). A block can never run longer than the count of available nonzero remainders, and here all six of \(1\) through \(6\) get used.

blocks.cap: Dividing \(1\) by \(7\), the leftover at each step rides around this ring in the order \(1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5\), and the quotient digit stamped on each arrow spells \(0.\overline{142857}\). The closing gold arrow from \(5\) back to \(1\) is the whole point. Every leftover is smaller than the divisor, so only finitely many leftovers are possible, and the moment one returns the digits are forced to repeat. The size of the loop is the length of the repeating block, the period. Here that loop holds six remainders, so the period is \(6\). Beside it, \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) loops straight back onto remainder \(1\) at once, a loop of one, giving the single digit block \(0.\overline{3}\).

blocks.x: Why decimals repeat. Long division prints each digit from a remainder, and it stops only when a remainder finally lands on $0$. But every remainder is smaller than the divisor $b$, so at most $b-1$ nonzero values can ever appear. If $0$ never shows up, some remainder must eventually return, and the instant it does, every later step copies an earlier one and the digits lock into a repeating block. That is why $\tfrac{1}{3}=0.\overline{3}$ and $\tfrac{1}{7}=0.\overline{142857}$, with the leftovers trapped in a loop. A fraction is always terminating or repeating, never random.
In \(\tfrac{1}{6} = 0.1\overline{6}\), only the \(6\) repeats. How many digits come before the repeating block begins, meaning how many are not under the bar?
hints: Write out the decimal with the bar in the right place. In \(0.1\overline{6}\), the bar covers the looping part. Everything to the left of where the bar starts is the non-repeating head. Just count those digits.
The repeating block is the \(6\), and the bar starts right at it. The only digit sitting before the bar is the \(1\). So count the digits before the loop begins.
blocks.sol: Divide \(1\) by \(6\). \(10 \div 6 = 1\) remainder \(4\), so the first digit is \(1\). Then \(40 \div 6 = 6\) remainder \(4\), the same remainder, so the \(6\) repeats from there. That gives \(\tfrac{1}{6} = 0.1\overline{6}\), and only \(\boxed{1}\) digit sits outside the bar. The head comes from the \(2\) in \(6 = 2 \times 3\). One factor of \(2\) buys one settling digit, and the \(3\) makes the loop.

blocks.x: The long division \(1 \div 11\) gives \(\tfrac{1}{11} = 0.\overline{09}\). The bar covers both the \(0\) and the \(9\). How many digits are in the repeating block? Give the period.
hints: The period is just a count. Look at the block sitting under the bar in \(0.\overline{09}\) and count its digits, including the leading zero.
The block is \(09\). Count its digits one at a time. There is a \(0\), and there is a \(9\). That is two digits.
blocks.sol: \(10 \div 11 = 0\) remainder \(10\), so the first digit after the point is \(0\). Then \(100 \div 11 = 9\) remainder \(1\), which is the remainder we began with, so the digits cycle as \(0, 9, 0, 9, \ldots\) and \(\tfrac{1}{11} = 0.\overline{09}\). The block \(09\) has \(\boxed{2}\) digits. Keep that leading zero, since \(0.\overline{9}\) is a completely different number.

blocks.x: Long division gives \(\tfrac{1}{12} = 0.08\overline{3}\). What is the repeating block? Type the digit or digits under the bar.
hints: The repeating block is the part that keeps coming back once the digits settle into their loop. The \(0\) and the \(8\) at the front each happen only once, so neither of them is part of the loop. Watch for the moment a remainder shows up a second time, because that is exactly when the repetition kicks in.

Carry the division out to \(0.0833333\ldots\). The remainder \(4\) appears, gives the digit \(3\), and then comes back as the remainder again, so the same step repeats and you keep writing \(3\). Only the \(3\) sits under the bar, so \(\tfrac{1}{12} = 0.08\overline{3}\).
blocks.sol: Divide \(1\) by \(12\). \(10 \div 12 = 0\) remainder \(10\), then \(100 \div 12 = 8\) remainder \(4\), then \(40 \div 12 = 3\) remainder \(4\). Remainder \(4\) has come back, so that step repeats forever and \(\tfrac{1}{12} = 0.08\overline{3}\). The block under the bar is \(\boxed{3}\). The head \(08\) is two digits because \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\) carries two factors of \(2\), and the \(3\) is what loops.

blocks.x: Which of \(\tfrac{1}{16}\), \(\tfrac{1}{20}\), \(\tfrac{1}{25}\), \(\tfrac{1}{15}\) repeats? Factor each denominator and apply the \(2\)s-and-\(5\)s test. Give the denominator.
hints: Break each denominator into primes. \(16 = 2^4\), \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\), \(25 = 5^2\), and \(15 = 3 \times 5\). The terminating ones use only the "friendly" primes \(2\) and \(5\). Look for the denominator that has a different prime.

Three of the denominators are made purely of \(2\)s and \(5\)s, so those three terminate. Only \(15 = 3 \times 5\) carries a prime that is neither \(2\) nor \(5\). That stray factor of \(3\) is what forces the digits to repeat, so the answer is its denominator.
blocks.sol: Factor the four denominators. \(16 = 2^4\), \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\), \(25 = 5^2\), and \(15 = 3 \times 5\). The first three are built only from \(2\)s and \(5\)s, so they terminate at \(0.0625\), \(0.05\), and \(0.04\). Only \(15\) carries a \(3\), and \(\tfrac{1}{15} = 0.0\overline{6}\), so the denominator is \(\boxed{15}\). Only \(2\) and \(5\) divide a power of ten, so any other prime can never be scaled away and the remainders cycle instead of reaching \(0\).

blocks.x: Read the decimal from the denominator. Factor the denominator of a fraction in lowest terms and you can predict its decimal before dividing. The $2$s and $5$s are the stopping primes, and whichever of those two counts is larger sets the length of a short non-repeating head. Every other prime is a looping prime that builds the repeating tail. So a denominator of only $2$s and $5$s gives a clean stop, a denominator with no $2$s or $5$s repeats from the very first digit, and a mix gives a short head and then a loop.

So far we have gone from a fraction to its repeating decimal. The trip back works too. Multiply by a power of ten to make a second copy of the same endless tail, subtract so the two tails cancel, and the infinite decimal collapses into an ordinary fraction.
Let \(x = 0.\overline{7}\). Multiply by \(10\) to get \(10x = 7.\overline{7}\). The tails of \(7\)s cancel when you subtract: \(9x = 7\). Write \(0.\overline{7}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: You built two equations, \(x = 0.7777\ldots\) and \(10x = 7.7777\ldots\). Stack the second over the first and subtract straight down. On the left you get \(10x - x\). On the right, the endless \(7\)s line up exactly and wipe each other out, so what whole number is left?
Subtracting gives \(9x = 7\). To get \(x\) by itself, divide both sides by \(9\). That leaves \(x = \tfrac{7}{9}\). Check whether \(7\) and \(9\) share any common factor before you call it done.
blocks.sol: Let \(x = 0.7777\ldots\), so \(10x = 7.7777\ldots\). Past the decimal point both numbers carry the identical endless string of \(7\)s, so subtracting wipes it out. $$10x - x = 7.7777\ldots - 0.7777\ldots$$ $$9x = 7$$ Divide by \(9\) to get \(x = \tfrac{7}{9}\), and \(7\) is prime so nothing reduces. $$\boxed{7/9}$$ Multiplying by \(10\) shifts past exactly one block, which is what lines the two tails up.

blocks.cap: Shifting by exactly one block length lines the endless tails up perfectly, so when you subtract they erase each other and an ordinary equation is left behind. Here \(10x - x = 7.\overline{7} - 0.\overline{7}\) gives \(9x = 7\), so \(0.\overline{7} = \tfrac{7}{9}\). The same trick scales to any pure repeater. A block of length \(k\) becomes the block written over \(k\) nines, for example \(0.\overline{12} = \tfrac{12}{99}\).

blocks.x: Let \(x = 0.\overline{12}\). Multiply by \(100\) to get \(100x = 12.\overline{12}\). Subtracting gives \(99x = 12\), so \(x = \tfrac{12}{99}\). Write \(0.\overline{12}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: You already know it begins as \(\tfrac{12}{99}\). Now ask the lowest-terms question. What whole number divides both \(12\) and \(99\) evenly?

Both \(12\) and \(99\) are divisible by \(3\). Divide the top and the bottom by \(3\), which gives \(12 \div 3 = 4\) and \(99 \div 3 = 33\). Check that \(4\) and \(33\) share no common factor, then you are finished.
blocks.sol: Let \(x = 0.121212\ldots\). The block is two digits, so multiply by \(100\). $$100x = 12.121212\ldots$$ The tails match, so subtracting leaves \(99x = 12\) and \(x = \tfrac{12}{99}\). Both parts are divisible by \(3\). $$\frac{12}{99} = \frac{4}{33}$$ Since \(4 = 2 \times 2\) and \(33 = 3 \times 11\), this is fully reduced, so \(0.\overline{12} = \boxed{4/33}\). The block-over-nines shortcut hands you a correct fraction but rarely a reduced one, so always check.

blocks.x: Let \(x = 0.\overline{9}\). Multiply by \(10\): \(10x = 9.\overline{9}\). Subtract: \(9x = 9\). Divide by \(9\). What does \(0.\overline{9}\) equal?
hints: You already did the hard part for \(0.\overline{7}\). Write \(x = 0.\overline{9}\) and \(10x = 9.\overline{9}\), then subtract. Trust the cancellation even though the result feels surprising.

Subtracting gives \(10x - x = 9.\overline{9} - 0.\overline{9}\). The infinite tails of nines are identical, so they vanish and leave \(9x = 9\). Now divide both sides by 9 and read off the single whole number you get.
blocks.sol: Let \(x = 0.9999\ldots\), so \(10x = 9.9999\ldots\). After the decimal point both numbers carry the same endless string of nines, so subtracting cancels it. $$10x - x = 9.9999\ldots - 0.9999\ldots$$ $$9x = 9$$ Divide by \(9\) and \(x = \boxed{1}\). Nothing was rounded or dropped anywhere in that work, so \(0.\overline{9}\) is not creeping up toward \(1\). It is another name for \(1\).

blocks.x: Write \(0.41\overline{6}\) as a fraction in lowest terms. Multiply by \(1{,}000\) and by \(100\), subtract to cancel the \(\overline{6}\) tails, then solve and reduce.
hints: You want two shifted copies of \(x\) whose decimal tails are identical, so the subtraction wipes the tail out. The repeating part is \(0.00\overline{6}\), sitting two places in. Try sliding the point so one copy stops just before the loop and the other stops just after one block of it.

Let \(x = 0.41\overline{6}\). Multiply by \(100\) to land just before the loop, \(100x = 41.\overline{6} = 41.666\ldots\). Multiply by \(1{,}000\) to land one block past it, \(1{,}000x = 416.\overline{6} = 416.666\ldots\). Both end in the same \(.666\ldots\) tail. Subtract the smaller from the larger and solve for \(x\), then reduce.
blocks.sol: Let \(x = 0.41666\ldots\). Shift past the head with \(100x = 41.666\ldots\), then one block further with \(1{,}000x = 416.666\ldots\). Both end in the same \(.666\ldots\) tail, so subtracting cancels it. $$1{,}000x - 100x = 416.666\ldots - 41.666\ldots$$ $$900x = 375$$ Then \(x = \tfrac{375}{900}\), and both share a factor of \(75\), since \(375 = 75 \cdot 5\) and \(900 = 75 \cdot 12\). $$x = \boxed{5/12}$$ When there is a non-repeating head you need two shifts, one landing just before the loop and one a full block later.

blocks.x: Turn a repeater back into a fraction. Shift by exactly one block length and subtract, so the endless tails line up and cancel, leaving a plain equation. A pure repeater becomes its block over a string of $9$s, one $9$ per digit: $0.\overline{7}=\tfrac{7}{9}$, $0.\overline{12}=\tfrac{12}{99}$, $0.\overline{481}=\tfrac{481}{999}$, then reduce. The same move settles a famous case. $0.\overline{9}=\tfrac{9}{9}=1$ exactly, not creeping toward $1$ but already there, since an endless decimal is one fixed number.
In base \(7\), the fraction \(\tfrac{1}{7}\) would simply be \(0.1\), while \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) would repeat. Whether a decimal terminates depends on the base, not the fraction.
\(\tfrac{1}{7} = 0.\overline{142857}\), a block of \(6\) digits. Divide \(50 \div 6\) to find the position within the block. What is the 50th digit after the decimal point?
hints: The block \(142857\) is six digits long, so the pattern resets every \(6\) positions. Every time you pass a full group of \(6\), you are back at the start of the block. So really you just need to know how far past the last full group position \(50\) sits.

Divide \(50\) by \(6\). You get \(8\) full blocks with \(2\) left over. That remainder of \(2\) tells you the \(50\)th digit is the same as the \(2\)nd digit of the block \(142857\). Read off the second digit.
blocks.sol: The block \(142857\) is six digits long, so divide. \(50 = 6 \times 8 + 2\), which puts position \(50\) two digits into a fresh block. The second digit of \(142857\) is \(\boxed{4}\). Only the remainder picks the digit. The quotient \(8\) just counts how many full blocks you skipped past.

blocks.x: Finding a far digit. Once you know the repeating block and its length, every digit is already determined, so finding the digit in some far position is just a matter of where that position lands inside the block. Divide the position by the period and read the remainder. Remainder $1$ means the first digit of the block, remainder $2$ the second, and remainder $0$ means you stopped on the last digit. No long division is needed beyond finding the period.
Find \(0.\overline{72} - 0.\overline{27}\) as a single fraction in lowest terms. Convert each to a fraction over \(99\), subtract, then reduce.
hints: Each of these has a two-digit repeating block, and you found a shortcut for exactly this. A repeating two-digit block sits over \(99\). So turn each decimal into a fraction with denominator \(99\) before you do anything else.

Once both are written over \(99\), they share a denominator, so you can subtract the top numbers directly and keep the \(99\) underneath. That leaves one fraction. Now reduce it by dividing the top and bottom by their greatest common factor.
blocks.sol: A two-digit block sits over \(99\), so \(0.\overline{72} = \tfrac{72}{99}\) and \(0.\overline{27} = \tfrac{27}{99}\). The denominators already match, so subtract the numerators. $$\frac{72}{99} - \frac{27}{99} = \frac{45}{99}$$ Both \(45\) and \(99\) are divisible by \(9\), which gives \(\tfrac{5}{11}\), and \(5\) shares no factor with \(11\). $$\boxed{5/11}$$ Checking, \(\tfrac{5}{11} = 0.\overline{45}\), and \(0.7272\ldots\) minus \(0.2727\ldots\) does leave \(0.4545\ldots\).

review.x: Long-divide \(2 \div 3\). Each step ends with the same remainder. What single digit repeats forever in the decimal \(0.\overline{6}\)?
hints: Notice that each step in the division leaves the same remainder of \(2\). When a remainder comes back, the next digit must be the same as the last one, so the decimal just loops.
The decimal is \(0.6666\ldots\), written compactly as \(0.\overline{6}\). The thing under the bar is the part that repeats.
review.sol: Since \(3\) is bigger than \(2\), the whole-number part is \(0\) and the remainder is \(2\). Then \(20 \div 3 = 6\) with remainder \(20 - 18 = 2\), the remainder we started with, so every step after that prints another \(6\). That makes \(2 \div 3 = 0.\overline{6}\), so the repeating digit is \(\boxed{6}\). A returning remainder is exactly what locks a decimal into a loop.

review.x: Long-divide \(1 \div 9\). The remainder returns immediately, giving \(\tfrac{1}{9} = 0.\overline{1}\). How many digits are in the repeating block? Give the period.
hints: The repeating block is whatever sits under the bar. Write out \(\tfrac{1}{9}\) as a decimal and look at what is covered.
In \(0.\overline{1}\) the bar sits over a single digit, the 1. Count how many digits are inside that block.
review.sol: Bring down a zero to get \(10\). Then \(10 \div 9 = 1\) with remainder \(1\), the number we started with, so every step writes another \(1\) and \(\tfrac{1}{9} = 0.\overline{1}\). The bar covers a single digit, so the period is \(\boxed{1}\).

review.x: Long-divide \(1 \div 11\). The remainder returns after two digits, giving \(\tfrac{1}{11} = 0.\overline{09}\). Write the repeating block as a digit string, including the leading zero.
hints: The block is the run of digits that repeats forever. You found two digits before the remainder returned to its starting value of \(1\), so the block is two digits long.
The first repeating digit came from \(11\) going into \(10\) zero times, and the second came from \(11\) going into \(100\) nine times. Keep that leading zero, the block is not just \(9\).
review.sol: Start with remainder \(1\). Attach a zero to get \(10\), and \(11\) fits into \(10\) zero times, so the first digit is \(0\) and the remainder is \(10\). Attach another zero to get \(100\), and \(11\) fits \(9\) times since \(9 \times 11 = 99\), leaving remainder \(1\) again. The digits cycle as \(0, 9, 0, 9, \ldots\), so the block is \(\boxed{09}\). The leading zero is part of the block, not decoration.

review.x: \(5 \div 6 = 0.8\overline{3}\). The digit \(8\) settles before the loop. How many digits come before the repeating block begins?
hints: Write the decimal out and mark the bar. In \(0.8\overline{3}\), the bar covers only the \(3\). Everything to the left of where the bar starts is the non-repeating head.
Look at the digits after the point one at a time. The \(8\) comes first and never repeats, then the \(3\) repeats forever. Count only the digits that live outside the bar.
review.sol: \(50 \div 6 = 8\) with remainder \(2\), so the first decimal digit is \(8\). Then \(20 \div 6 = 3\) with remainder \(2\) again, so the \(3\) loops from there and \(\tfrac{5}{6} = 0.8\overline{3}\). Exactly \(\boxed{1}\) digit sits outside the bar. A decimal like this is called eventually repeating, since it settles into its loop after a short run-up instead of right away.

review.x: Long-divide \(7 \div 30\) to find \(\tfrac{7}{30} = 0.2\overline{3}\). The \(2\) settles first. What single digit is the repeating block?
hints: Carry out the long division of \(7 \div 30\). Watch the remainders. Once a remainder shows up a second time, the digits from that point on will repeat forever.
The first digit \(2\) settles and is gone for good. After that one digit keeps coming back. That recurring digit is the whole repeating block.
review.sol: \(70 \div 30 = 2\) with remainder \(10\), so the first decimal digit is \(2\). Then \(100 \div 30 = 3\) with remainder \(10\), the same remainder, so every later step writes another \(3\). That gives \(\tfrac{7}{30} = 0.2\overline{3}\), so the repeating block is \(\boxed{3}\). The \(2\) and the \(5\) in \(30\) produce the one settling digit, and the \(3\) produces the loop.

review.x: Let \(x = 0.\overline{5}\). Multiply by \(10\): \(10x = 5.\overline{5}\). Subtract: \(9x = 5\). Write \(0.\overline{5}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: You have \(9x = 5\) after the subtraction. To get \(x\) by itself, divide both sides by \(9\).
Dividing gives \(x = \tfrac{5}{9}\). Check whether \(5\) and \(9\) share any common factor before you call it final.
review.sol: Let \(x = 0.5555\ldots\), so \(10x = 5.5555\ldots\). Both numbers end in the identical endless string of fives, so subtracting cancels the tails and leaves \(9x = 5\). Divide by \(9\) to get \(x = \tfrac{5}{9}\), and since \(9 = 3 \times 3\) shares nothing with \(5\), it is already in lowest terms. \(\boxed{5/9}\)

review.x: Using the block-over-nines shortcut, \(0.\overline{2}\) has a one-digit block, so it equals \(\tfrac{2}{9}\). Write \(0.\overline{2}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The block is one digit long, so the denominator is a single \(9\). Start by writing the block over that nine and you have \(\tfrac{2}{9}\).
Now check whether \(\tfrac{2}{9}\) can shrink. A fraction reduces only when the top and bottom share a common factor bigger than \(1\). What divides both \(2\) and \(9\)?
review.sol: The block is one digit, so it goes over a single nine, and \(0.\overline{2} = \tfrac{2}{9}\). The factors of \(2\) are \(1\) and \(2\), the factors of \(9\) are \(1\), \(3\), and \(9\), so they share only \(1\) and the fraction cannot shrink. \(\boxed{2/9}\) That nine is really \(10 - 1\). Setting \(x = 0.\overline{2}\) and subtracting gives \(10x - x = 9x = 2\).

review.x: The decimal \(0.\overline{81}\) equals \(\tfrac{81}{99}\). Reduce \(\tfrac{81}{99}\) to lowest terms. What fraction do you get?
hints: A repeating block of length two always sits over \(99\), which is why \(0.\overline{81}=\dfrac{81}{99}\). Now ask what number divides into both \(81\) and \(99\).
Both \(81\) and \(99\) are multiples of \(9\). Divide the top and the bottom by \(9\) and see what is left.
review.sol: A two-digit block sits over \(99\), so \(0.\overline{81} = \tfrac{81}{99}\). The greatest common factor of \(81\) and \(99\) is \(9\), since \(81 = 9 \times 9\) and \(99 = 9 \times 11\). Dividing top and bottom by \(9\) gives \(\boxed{9/11}\). Checking, \(9 \div 11 = 0.818181\ldots\). The block-over-nines shortcut gives a correct value but rarely a reduced one.

review.x: Write \(0.0\overline{45}\) as a fraction in lowest terms. Use \(1{,}000x\) and \(10x\) to cancel the repeating tails, giving \(990x = 45\), then reduce.
hints: The repeating block starts at the second decimal place, not the first. Use the multiplier that jumps past everything once, \(1{,}000x\), and the one that jumps past just the leading zero, \(10x\), so their tails match.
After \(1{,}000x = 45.4545\ldots\) and \(10x = 0.4545\ldots\), subtract to get \(990x = 45\), so \(x = \tfrac{45}{990}\). Now find the greatest common factor of \(45\) and \(990\) and divide it out.
review.sol: Let \(x = 0.0454545\ldots\). Shift three places to land just before a fresh block, \(1{,}000x = 45.4545\ldots\), and one place to clear the head zero, \(10x = 0.4545\ldots\). Both end in the same \(.4545\ldots\) tail, so subtracting gives \(990x = 45\) and \(x = \tfrac{45}{990}\). Both share \(45\), since \(990 = 45 \cdot 22\), so \(x = \boxed{1/22}\). The leading zero appears once and never repeats, which is why a single shift will not line the tails up.

review.x: Let \(x = 0.\overline{9}\). Multiply by \(10\): \(10x = 9.\overline{9}\). Subtract and solve. What single whole number does \(0.\overline{9}\) equal?
hints: You already have \(9x = 9\). Divide both sides by \(9\) to get \(x\) all by itself.
Both the starting decimal and the answer are the same number \(x\), so whatever \(x\) turns out to be is exactly what \(0.\overline{9}\) is. It is a single whole number, not a fraction.
review.sol: Let \(x = 0.\overline{9}\), so \(10x = 9.\overline{9}\). After the decimal point both carry the identical endless string of nines, so subtracting cancels it and leaves \(9x = 9\). Divide by \(9\) and \(x = \boxed{1}\). A second check agrees. \(0.\overline{1} = \tfrac{1}{9}\), and nine copies give \(\tfrac{9}{9} = 1\) while \(9 \cdot 0.\overline{1} = 0.\overline{9}\).

review.x: \(\tfrac{1}{13} = 0.\overline{076923}\), a block of \(6\) digits. Divide \(100 \div 6\) to place the position within the block. What is the 100th digit after the decimal point?
hints: The digits repeat in groups of six, \(076923\). After every full group of six digits you are back at the start, so positions \(6\), \(12\), \(18\), and so on all hold the last digit of the block. Ask where position \(100\) sits relative to a fresh group.
Divide \(100\) by \(6\). You get \(16\) whole groups with a remainder of \(4\), since \(16 \times 6 = 96\) and \(100 - 96 = 4\). So the 100th digit is the 4th digit of the block \(076923\).
review.sol: The block \(076923\) is six digits long, so divide. \(100 = 6 \times 16 + 4\), since \(6 \times 16 = 96\), which puts position \(100\) four digits into a fresh block. Reading \(076923\), the 4th digit is \(\boxed{9}\). The quotient \(16\) only counts the full blocks that went by. The remainder is what picks the digit.
review.label: r11

review.x: \(\frac{4}{33} = 0.\overline{12}\), a block of \(2\) digits. Divide \(99 \div 2\) to find the position in the block. What is the 99th digit after the decimal point?
hints: The digits repeat with a block of length \(2\). The odd positions \(1, 3, 5, \ldots\) all hold one digit, and the even positions \(2, 4, 6, \ldots\) all hold the other. Which kind of position is \(99\)?
Divide \(99\) by the block length \(2\). The remainder tells you how far into the block you land. A remainder of \(1\) points at the first digit of \(12\).
review.sol: The block \(12\) is two digits long, so divide. \(99 = 2 \times 49 + 1\), so position \(99\) lands on the first digit of the block, which is \(\boxed{1}\). With a block of length \(2\), odd positions all hold the \(1\) and even positions all hold the \(2\), and \(99\) is odd.

review.x: Factor each denominator: \(8=2^3\), \(40=2^3\times5\), \(50=2\times5^2\), \(24=2^3\times3\). Which denominator contains a prime other than \(2\) or \(5\), forcing its decimal to repeat?
hints: A fraction terminates only if, in lowest terms, its denominator is made of 2s and 5s and nothing else. Three of these pass. Look for the one factorization that has a different prime.
Scan the four factorizations for a prime that is not 2 and not 5. Only \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\) carries a 3, so that 3 is what forces the repeat.
review.sol: Read the factorizations. \(8 = 2^3\), \(40 = 2^3 \times 5\), and \(50 = 2 \times 5^2\) use only \(2\)s and \(5\)s, so all three terminate. \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\) carries a \(3\), which is neither \(2\) nor \(5\), so the repeating denominator is \(\boxed{24}\). Its decimal is \(\tfrac{1}{24} = 0.041\overline{6}\), and that stray \(3\) is the reason it never ends.

review.x: Find \(0.\overline{81} - 0.\overline{36}\) as a single fraction in lowest terms. Both two-digit repeaters sit over \(99\). Subtract the numerators and reduce.
hints: A two-digit repeating block sits over two nines. So \(0.\overline{81}=\tfrac{81}{99}\) and \(0.\overline{36}=\tfrac{36}{99}\). Now you have two fractions that share the same bottom.
When the denominators already match, you only subtract the tops. Work out \(81-36\), keep \(99\) underneath, then look for a common factor to reduce the result.
review.sol: A two-digit block sits over \(99\), so \(0.\overline{81} = \tfrac{81}{99}\) and \(0.\overline{36} = \tfrac{36}{99}\). The denominators match, so subtract the numerators. $$\frac{81}{99} - \frac{36}{99} = \frac{45}{99}$$ Both \(45\) and \(99\) are divisible by \(9\), since \(45 = 9 \times 5\) and \(99 = 9 \times 11\), so the answer is \(\boxed{5/11}\). Checking, \(5 \div 11 = 0.\overline{45}\), exactly the gap between the two decimals.
